title: Valdez Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Valdez wells have a 300-foot median depth, 3.3 gpm median yield, and finished costs of about $16,500-$28,500.
h1: Valdez, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Valdez means evaluating more than whether a permit exists. The local records show 647 permitted wells within 5 miles, with 544 recorded as constructed. Only 112 report a total depth, 25 report a pump yield, and 4 report a static water level, so the database is useful for local patterns but cannot predict every lot.

For planning, the area has a 300-foot median well depth and a 3.3-gpm median reported yield. Most permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers rather than Denver Basin aquifers. Use nearby well records, a site evaluation, and a written driller's estimate before committing to a purchase or building plan.

sections.heading: What Valdez well depths look like
sections.html:
Reported Valdez wells have a median depth of 300 feet. The middle half falls from 118 to 480 feet, and the 90th percentile reaches 606 feet. The deepest record is 1,000 feet. That spread matters when comparing drilling bids: a price based only on the median may not cover a hole that follows the deeper local pattern.

Depths are mixed across the area. Eighteen percent are under 100 feet, 30% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 39% fall from 300 to 600 feet, and 12% are 600 feet or deeper. The ground is described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, while permits most often name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Fractured rock can be unpredictable over short distances, so a nearby shallow well is not a guarantee for a new lot.

sections.heading: How much water Valdez wells produce
sections.html:
The reported yield median is 3.3 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 1.5 to 6.5 gallons per minute. Fifty-two percent of reported yields are from 1 to 5 gallons per minute, 36% from 5 to 15, 4% above 15, and 8% under 1. These figures describe tested or reported well performance, not a promise for an unbuilt well.

A yield around the local median can support ordinary household use when the pressure system and storage are designed properly, but a buyer should not equate a modest pumping rate with unlimited water. Ask for the well yield, recovery information, pump size, and intended use. Colorado exempt household-use wells are generally limited to household purposes and the applicable pumping rules, including the 35-gpm exempt-well limit.

sections.heading: Valdez water levels and what the records show
sections.html:
Only 4 Valdez-area records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is small. Among those records, the median depth to water is 277 feet, and the middle half runs from 226 to 399 feet. That is useful for thinking about pump setting and construction, but it is not enough evidence to establish a broad water-table trend.

The permit history also does not provide a decade-by-decade static-water-level series. In practical terms, the available facts do not show that the water table is rising or dropping across Valdez. Have a driller review neighboring completion reports and measure an existing well when possible. A well with adequate production can still require substantial pumping equipment if the water level is deep.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Valdez, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity is concentrated in recent decades. The records list 7 permits from the 1950s, 3 from the 1960s, 4 from the 1970s, 2 from the 1980s, 83 from the 1990s, 36 from the 2000s, 456 from the 2010s, and 5 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Boday Well Drilling appears most often under Alex Boday, with 40 records, and under Kathleen Boday, with 24. Owner-listed drilling accounts for 18 records. These names show who appears in the permit history, not necessarily who is available or appropriate for a current job. Before relying on an old well, pull the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit and construction record, then confirm the current pump, casing, grout, production, and legal use.

sections.heading: What a new Valdez well may cost
sections.html:
For Valdez's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the local drilling model uses about $35 to $55 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models to roughly $10,500 to $16,500. That is a planning range, not a fixed quote; depth, casing, grout, access, water conditions, and site logistics can move the final number.

A finished system including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $16,500 to $28,500 at the median depth. Ask whether a bid includes mobilization, permit work, casing, grout, development, testing, electrical service, and connection to the house. A deeper-than-typical hole or difficult access near Cokedale, Segundo, or other surrounding areas can require a revised estimate.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
Low yield is the main practical concern in this record set: 8% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute, while most fall in the 1-to-5-gpm range. Dry holes and weak fractures are possible concerns in fractured-bedrock settings, so review nearby wells rather than relying on one favorable record. Also confirm that the existing permit allows the use you plan.

Environmental review matters around Valdez. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 220 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 171 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the supplied data, but that does not replace testing. Test raw well water for appropriate local concerns, and evaluate septic setbacks, soil, drainage, access for drilling equipment, and the proposed building location before closing or excavating.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Valdez lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's legal water path. Search Colorado DWR records for the property and nearby wells, confirm the permit type and allowed uses, and obtain construction and pump information for any existing well. Compare several neighboring wells rather than using the 300-foot median or 3.3-gpm median as a guarantee.

For vacant land, get a driller to review access, likely depth, casing and grout requirements, pump setting, and the cost range before you make the purchase decision. Leave room for the well, septic system, house, driveway, and future repairs. If the lot is near Cokedale, Segundo, Jansen, Starkville, Trinidad, or Weston, use those areas as context only; the individual parcel and its geology control the result.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Valdez, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Valdez is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 118 to 480 feet, while the 90th percentile is 606 feet and the deepest record is 1,000 feet. Depth varies substantially, so a nearby well can help a driller estimate conditions but cannot guarantee the depth on a new parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Valdez?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses about $35 to $55 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $10,500 to $16,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $16,500 to $28,500. A deeper hole, difficult access, or added site work can change the quote.

faq.q: How much water do Valdez wells produce?
faq.a: Reported wells near Valdez have a median yield of 3.3 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 1.5 to 6.5 gallons per minute. Fifty-two percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and 8% report under 1. These are reported results from 25 wells, not a guarantee for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Valdez, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from the permit map alone. The area has 220 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 171 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing well for appropriate contaminants, inspect the wellhead and septic layout, and retest if conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: Are there water-level concerns near Valdez?
faq.a: Only 4 records report static water levels. Their median depth to water is 277 feet, with the middle half from 226 to 399 feet. That small sample does not establish a rising or falling regional trend. Have a driller inspect nearby records and existing equipment, because a deep water level affects pump selection and total installation cost.
